title: The Sacred Band of Thebes
text:
In the 370s BC Thebes formed an elite unit of three hundred chosen soldiers, kept and trained at public expense. Plutarch, in his Life of Pelopidas, says it was first organized by Gorgidas, and that it was made up of pairs of lovers. He quotes the Theban general Pammenes, who said Homer was wrong to group soldiers by tribe and family: men of the same clan care little for each other in danger, but a band bound by love will not break, because each man is ashamed to act basely in front of the one he loves.

At first Gorgidas spread the Band thinly across the front ranks of the army. Pelopidas, after seeing them fight alone and win against a larger Spartan force at Tegyra in 375 BC, never divided them again. He kept them together as one body and gave them the hardest assignments in the great battles. Plutarch compares them to horses that run faster harnessed together than alone, each spurring the others on. They played a key part in the Theban victory over Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC.

Plutarch says the Band was never defeated until the battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC, when Philip of Macedon crushed Thebes and Athens. Walking over the field afterward, Philip found the three hundred lying dead together where they had faced his phalanx. Told who they were, he wept and said: "Perish any man who suspects that these men either did or suffered anything that was base."
lesson: Units hold under pressure when members care about each other personally, not just about the mission. Keep close teams together rather than scattering them.
people: Gorgidas, Pelopidas, Philip II of Macedon
caveat: Ancient authors give the Band only brief mention, and some details of its composition rest on Plutarch alone.
